Pratfall. An exaggerated tumble, stumble, or fall performed for comedic effect—one of the basic units of physical comedy in slapstick and silent film. The term derives from the commedia dell'arte tradition and specifically from the slap sound made by a prop stick, or slapstick, striking the stage. In cinema, the pratfall became a fundamental gag, requiring precise control of timing, positioning, and camera framing to land the joke.

Pratfalls appear in commedia dell'arte, Renaissance Italian street theater, and music-hall traditions, where they were improvised responses to audience energy. Cinema rendered them precisely choreographed and reproducible. In silent film, the pratfall's effectiveness depends on three elements. The performer's apparent loss of control, the appearance of accident. The camera's framing, showing the full body or the impact point. And the audience's complicity in recognizing the physical effort required to make it look unintentional.

Buster Keaton was the master of the pratfall. His deadpan expression while falling made the gag sublime. The audience laughs not at falling but at the contrast between his impassive face and the chaos of his body. Pratfalls require extraordinary physical control. A performer must absorb impact safely while appearing to surrender to gravity, and the fall must be reproducible across multiple takes for editing. The vertical pratfall—falling straight backward or forward—differs from the horizontal pratfall, a sliding tumble across ground or furniture. Each requires different technical skill and timing.

Silent film elevated pratfalls from improvisational theater into precisely choreographed sequences. Keaton could design an entire scene around a single, complex pratfall, where every element—furniture placement, camera angle, actor position—was predetermined. The pratfall's decline coincides with sound cinema's rise. Dialogue-based comedy made physical gags seem crude, and performers trained in dialogue acting often lacked the bodily control pratfalls required.
